action.rationale: Vectorize the j inner loop with width 4 (float4 = 128 bits). This uses LDG.128 instructions, the widest load unit on Ampere, halving the number of memory transactions and improving L2/DRAM throughput utilization for this BW-bound elementwise op.

decisions.rationale: Tile the outer i-dimension by 32 to create 512/32=16 outer tiles. This exposes parallelism across the 30 SMs on Ampere; each tile maps to a CUDA thread block, giving ~16 blocks along i that can be spread across SMs.

Tile j by 128 to create inner tiles of 128 elements. This aligns with 128-byte cache lines (32 fp32 elements) × 4 = 128-element vector chunks, enabling coalesced 128-bit LDG.128 loads. Each tile fits nicely in registers without spilling on Ampere's 65536-register file.

Map the tiled i outer loop to threadblock.x so each block of 32 rows is processed by a distinct CUDA block. With 512/32=16 tiles along i and 512/128=4 tiles along j, we get 16×4=64 blocks — more than enough to saturate 30 SMs with 2 waves.

Map the j tile loop to warps within each block. Each 128-element j-tile is handled by warps in lockstep — with 128/32=4 warps per block, this gives 4×32=128 threads per block doing coalesced 32-element (128-byte) warp-level memory transactions.

Vectorize the j inner loop with width 4 (float4 = 128 bits). This uses LDG.128 instructions, the widest load unit on Ampere, halving the number of memory transactions and improving L2/DRAM throughput utilization for this BW-bound elementwise op.

action.rationale: Tile the inner reduction loop (N=2048) into chunks of 1024. This splits the 2048-element reduction into two phases of 1024 elements each, fitting comfortably in the 49152 bytes of shared memory (1024 * 4 bytes = 4KB per row tile), enabling staged two-pass mean+variance computation with good register reuse.

decisions.rationale: Tile the outer row loop (M=64) into chunks of 32. With 30 SMs on Ampere, 64/32=2 tiles — each tile covers 32 rows, keeping 2 concurrent waves across SMs. This exposes enough parallelism without over-fragmenting work, and aligns well to warp-multiple boundaries.

Tile the inner reduction loop (N=2048) into chunks of 1024. This splits the 2048-element reduction into two phases of 1024 elements each, fitting comfortably in the 49152 bytes of shared memory (1024 * 4 bytes = 4KB per row tile), enabling staged two-pass mean+variance computation with good register reuse.

Map each row (i) to a distinct thread block (threadblock.x). LayerNorm is embarrassingly parallel across rows — each row is independent. With M=64 rows and 30 SMs, this gives ~2 waves of 32 blocks each, saturating the GPU. This is the canonical high-performance layernorm pattern: one CTA per row handles the full reduction over N=2048.

Vectorize the inner j-loop with width 4 (float4 / 128-bit loads). N=2048 is divisible by 4, enabling coalesced 128-bit memory transactions. This reduces the number of memory instructions by 4×, maximizing memory bandwidth utilization on Ampere's L2/HBM. Width-4 is the sweet spot for FP32 (4×4B = 16B = 128-bit, matching cache line granularity).

Tile the M-dimension (i) with factor 128. A 128-row block tile is the standard GEMM output-block height for Ampere, balancing register pressure and occupancy while producing enough work per CTA (128×128 = 16K output elements) to hide memory latency across 30 SMs.

Tile the N-dimension (j) with factor 128 to match the i-tile. A 128×128 output block per CTA maximizes data reuse in shared memory (A tile: 128×32, B tile: 32×128, both fit in 48 KB), and 64 CTAs (1024/128)² fill all 30 SMs ~2× for good wave occupancy.

Map the M-dimension (i) tiles to threadblock.y. This assigns each 128-row output tile to a distinct CTA row, enabling all 30 SMs to execute CTAs concurrently. Separating i→y and j→x avoids threadblock dimension conflicts and matches standard row-major GEMM CTA grid layout.

Map the N-dimension (j) tiles to threadblock.x. This creates a 2D CTA grid of (M/128) × (N/128) = 8×8 = 64 CTAs, providing ~2 waves over 30 SMs for good utilization. threadblock.x for the column dimension is conventional for coalesced global-memory access to B.

Vectorize the j (N) inner loop with width 8. For FP16, width-8 maps to 128-bit (float4) vector loads/stores from global memory, maximizing memory bandwidth utilization. This also enables the compiler to generate efficient LDG.128 instructions on Ampere.

action.rationale: Tile the K-reduction axis with factor 16. A k-tile of 16 means each iteration loads a 64×16 slice of A and a 16×64 slice of B into shared memory (64×16 + 16×64 = 2048 fp32 elements = 8KB, well within 49KB), then accumulates into the 64×64 register tile. 16 steps of 16 across the K=256 dimension gives 16 pipelineable stages — small enough to hide latency without over-subscribing registers.

decisions.rationale: Tile the M-dimension (i) with factor 64. A 64-row tile per thread-block is a standard choice for Ampere GEMM — it keeps each CTA working on a 64×64 output tile, giving enough reuse to amortize shared-memory loads while keeping register pressure manageable. 256/64 = 4 tiles along M, which distributes well across 30 SMs.

Tile the N-dimension (j) with factor 64 to match the i-tile. A symmetric 64×64 output tile per CTA is the textbook blocked-GEMM configuration: both A-tile (64×k_tile) and B-tile (k_tile×64) fit in the 49KB shared memory, maximises data reuse on both operands, and produces a square output tile that maps cleanly to warp-level MMA layouts on Ampere.

Tile the K-reduction axis with factor 16. A k-tile of 16 means each iteration loads a 64×16 slice of A and a 16×64 slice of B into shared memory (64×16 + 16×64 = 2048 fp32 elements = 8KB, well within 49KB), then accumulates into the 64×64 register tile. 16 steps of 16 across the K=256 dimension gives 16 pipelineable stages — small enough to hide latency without over-subscribing registers.

Switch to a 32-row tile on i. For a 256×256 problem, 64×64 tiles yielded only 16 CTAs (under-utilizing 30 SMs). With tile=32 on both i and j we get 8×8=64 CTAs, spreading work across all 30 SMs with ~2 waves, far better occupancy than the 64-based strategy.

Symmetric 32-column tile on j to pair with the 32-row i-tile. The 32×32 output tile fits cleanly within warp-level MMA fragments on Ampere and keeps the shared-memory footprint (32×16 + 16×32 = 1024 fp32 = 4KB) well within 49KB budget, leaving headroom for double-buffering later.

action.rationale: Vectorize the j (N) inner loop with width 4 to issue 128-bit (4×fp32) or 256-bit wide memory loads/stores. This saturates memory bandwidth and maps to LDG.128 instructions on Ampere, giving 4× throughput on B-matrix loads and C-matrix stores while keeping register pressure manageable.

decisions.rationale: Tile the M-dimension with factor 128 to create 512/128=4 tiles. This matches a typical GEMM block size that fits comfortably in the 49KB shared memory while giving enough work per tile to hide latency. 128 is a canonical GEMM tile size for Ampere.

Tile the N-dimension with factor 128 to create a 128×128 output tile per thread block. Combined with the i-tile of 128, each block computes a 128×128 output region. This maximizes arithmetic intensity (128*128 outputs vs 2*128*K loads) and is the standard Ampere GEMM block shape that fits in shared memory (128*128*2 bytes ≈ 32KB for fp16, well under 49KB).

Tile the K reduction axis with factor 32 to enable software pipelining of shared memory loads. A k-tile of 32 with 128×128 output block means each stage loads 128×32 + 32×128 = 8192 elements into shared memory (32KB for fp16), fitting within the 49KB budget. This is the standard Ampere GEMM stage size that enables double-buffering and hides memory latency.

Map the i (M) outer-tile loop to threadblock.y so each thread block handles a different row-tile. With 512/128=4 tiles in M and 4 in N, this creates a 4×4=16 threadblock grid covering all 30 SMs efficiently. Using .y for the M dimension follows the row-major convention and improves L2 cache locality for A-matrix accesses.

Map the j (N) outer-tile loop to threadblock.x so columns are spread across the x-dimension of the grid. Combined with i→threadblock.y, we get a 2D 4×4 threadblock grid launching 16 blocks across 30 SMs. The x-dimension for j aligns with contiguous column access in row-major B, improving memory coalescing.

Vectorize the j (N) inner loop with width 4 to issue 128-bit (4×fp32) or 256-bit wide memory loads/stores. This saturates memory bandwidth and maps to LDG.128 instructions on Ampere, giving 4× throughput on B-matrix loads and C-matrix stores while keeping register pressure manageable.

Tile the outer `i` dimension by 128 to create 8 independent row-groups (1024/128=8). This maps cleanly to the 30-SM device, giving 8×(j-tiles) thread-blocks that can be scheduled across SMs. 128 rows per tile also keeps L1 reuse high for elementwise ops.

Tile the inner `j` dimension by 128 to create 8 column-groups (1024/128=8). With 128 elements per tile, we get 64 total thread-blocks (8×8), which is 2× the SM count (30), ensuring good wave occupancy. The 128-wide inner tile will allow vectorized 128-bit loads (4×float32) along `j`.

Vectorize the `j` loop with width=4 to emit 128-bit vector loads/stores (float4). The `j` axis is the contiguous (row-major) dimension, so 4×float32 = 128-bit aligned accesses match the Ampere L1/L2 cache line structure and maximize memory bandwidth utilization for this memory-bound elementwise kernel.

Map tiled `i` outer loop to threadblock.x so each tile of 128 rows becomes an independent GPU thread-block. Combined with the `j` tiling, this generates 8×8=64 thread-blocks total — about 2 full waves across 30 SMs — keeping all SMs busy and hiding launch/scheduling overhead.

action.rationale: Tiling the reduction axis `j` with 1024 threads per tile matches the max_threads_per_block=1024 on Ampere. For a 4096-wide row, this creates 4 chunks that can be reduced with efficient warp-shuffle + shared-memory tree reductions. 1024 elements × 4 bytes = 4 KB per tile, well within the 49 KB shared memory budget.

decisions.rationale: Each of the 64 rows is independent; mapping row-loop `i` to parallel GPU thread-blocks lets all 30 SMs contribute and eliminates sequential row iteration. With 64 rows and 30 SMs this gives ~2 waves — close to full utilisation.

For a 4096-wide row, this creates 4 chunks that can be reduced with efficient warp-shuffle + shared-memory tree reductions. 1024 elements × 4 bytes = 4 KB per tile, well within the 49 KB shared memory budget.

Vectorizing the inner reduction loop `j` with width=4 enables 128-bit memory loads (float4), which is the optimal load width on Ampere for FP32. This improves memory bandwidth utilization for the row-wise read pattern and reduces instruction count by 4×.
